rationale: The prayer that God remember His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob repeats the three ancestors and divine remembering at the beginning of Israel's rescue from Egypt.
The request for a heart willing to revere God and do His wishes resembles the promised divine cleansing of the heart followed by obedience to His commandments.
The prayer for an opened heart toward God's law corresponds to Deuteronomy's connection between divine heart renewal and keeping the written commandments.
The request that God hear and be reconciled to the recipients resembles Solomon's petition that God hear His displaced people from heaven and be merciful to their wrongs.
The letter traces the crisis to Jason and his associates; the narrative describes Jason's acquisition of the priesthood and his replacement of lawful civic life with Greek customs.
The letter's sacrifices, lamps, and loaves correspond to the specific acts of restored temple worship narrated after the sanctuary's purification.
Both accounts specifically include relighting the lamps and returning the loaves to their proper place in the restored temple.
The invitation to observe Booths in Chislev concerns the purification celebration described as eight days in the manner of Booths and decreed for annual observance.
The proposed observance on the twenty-fifth of Chislev matches the later narrative's purification date and annual festival decree; the Nehemiah fire tradition is additional material in the letter.
The following chapter expressly refers back to the preservation of altar fire at the deportation, adding Jeremiah's instruction to take it.
Nehemiah's being sent by the Persian king corresponds to his commission to return to Judah and rebuild; Nehemiah's own account does not narrate recovery of thick water or altar fire.
Sprinkling water on the offering and wood before a remarkable fire resembles Elijah's drenched offering consumed by divine fire; the liquids and narrative explanations differ.
The unexpected ignition and the spectators' amazement resemble the fire consuming Elijah's wet offering and the people's recognition of God, without equating the two events.
Calling Israel God's portion and asking its sanctification resembles Solomon's prayer identifying Israel as God's people and inheritance set apart from the nations.
The request to gather the scattered people and release those among the nations corresponds to the law's promise of mercy, gathering, and return to the inherited land.
The plea for the scattered people to be gathered resembles Nehemiah's prayer invoking Moses' promise that even the farthest dispersed will return to God's chosen place.
The request to plant the people in the holy place expressly invokes Moses and corresponds to his song asking God to plant His people on the mountain of His inheritance.
Water poured over stones after the sacrifice recalls the unusual combination of water, stones, and altar fire in Elijah's offering; it does not establish a shared event or identical mechanism.
The report to the Persian king expressly recapitulates the hidden fire, recovered water, and purification described earlier in the letter.
The words as has been indicated refer back to the deported priests' preservation of altar fire in the preceding account.
Jeremiah's reported warning not to forget the ordinances or be led astray by images parallels Moses' linked warnings against forgetting what was taught and making or worshiping visible likenesses.
The instruction not to let the law depart from the heart resembles Moses' warning that the remembered revelation must not depart from the heart throughout life.
The mountain where Moses viewed the inheritance is the setting of Moses' ascent and the Lord's display of the promised land; Deuteronomy does not recount Jeremiah's visit.
Jeremiah's reported expectation that God gather His people and become merciful uses the combination of mercy and gathering promised in the law.
The expected glory and cloud expressly recall Moses' time, when the cloud covered the tent and God's glory filled it.
The reference to Solomon's sanctuary is illuminated by the dedication account in which a cloud of the Lord's glory fills the temple and prevents priestly service.
Solomon's dedication sacrifices are narrated with the offerings of the king and people and the dedication of God's house.

The recalled fire in Moses' time corresponds to Moses and Aaron's appearance before the people and the fire from the Lord consuming the altar offerings; Leviticus does not quote the prayer mentioned here.
Solomon finishes praying and fire descends from heaven to consume the offerings, the precise sequence recalled here.

The statement about the uneaten sin offering recalls Moses' discovery that the goat had been burned and his question why the priests had not eaten it; it is a compressed recollection of that exchange.
The recollection of Solomon's eight days corresponds to the seven-day feast with its eighth-day closing celebration; the target preserves the separate day and dismissal notices.

Judas's recovery of scattered writings answers the documented crisis in which books of the law were destroyed and possession of the covenant book was punished; scattering and burning are not identical losses.
The renewed invitation to observe purification repeats the letter's earlier announcement of the twenty-fifth-of-Chislev observance.

The statement that God restored the people's inheritance corresponds to the law's promise to gather them and return them to the land inherited by their fathers; this target does not separately specify restored kingship or priesthood.
The hope of gathering from under heaven to the holy place expressly appeals to the law and closely follows its promise to gather even those dispersed to heaven's farthest end.
The announced topic of Judas's purification of the temple and dedication of the altar is carried out in the subsequent account of recovery, cleansing, and a new altar.
The introductory naming of Epiphanes and Eupator corresponds to the later formal transition from Epiphanes' death to the wars under his son Eupator.
The introduction's heavenly manifestations are exemplified by the five mounted figures protecting Maccabeus and striking the enemy during battle.
The introductory claim that the ancestral laws were restored is supported by Eupator's later letter permitting ancestral customs and restoring the temple to the Jews.
The author's intention to benefit and delight readers is revisited in the closing assessment of the composition and its comparison of pleasing prose to mixed wine.
The stated pursuit of concise expression corresponds to the closing wish that the work be well composed and to the point.
The initial peace under Onias is broken by Simon's continuing accusations and violent rivalry, which lead Onias to seek royal intervention for public peace.
The royal gifts honouring the temple are later explicitly identified as objects Antiochus removes with profane hands.
Seleucus's payment of sacrificial expenses resembles the Persian decree supplying temple costs and daily sacrificial materials from royal revenues; these are distinct kings and grants.
Simon's dispute with Onias develops into the next chapter's accusations and killings, explicitly attributed to the same informer and his supporters.
Simon's claim that the funds are available for royal seizure is answered by Onias's identification of protected private deposits and rejection of confiscation.
The later narrator explicitly remembers Heliodorus as Seleucus's agent sent to inspect the treasury, the mission initiated here.
Onias's identification of funds belonging to widows and orphans places the threatened seizure against the law's express protection of those groups and assurance that God hears their cry.
The named private owner and counted deposits correct Simon's report of uncountable funds available to the king; the text itself calls his report a misrepresentation.
Onias's refusal to allow injustice to depositors accords with the law condemning deceit concerning deposits and requiring entrusted property to be returned.
The city's anguish at the planned treasury seizure is explicitly reversed when the narrator describes the formerly fearful temple filled with gladness after divine intervention.
The priests invoke the One who legislated concerning deposits; Exodus supplies laws governing entrusted money, property, dishonesty, and restitution.
Leviticus likewise specifically forbids wrongdoing concerning a deposit and requires its return, supplying legal substance for the priests' prayer for depositors.
The public entreaty with hands extended during the temple crisis resembles Solomon's provision for afflicted people stretching out hands toward the house and seeking God's hearing.
The prayer that entrusted property remain safe addresses the specific responsibility for deposits regulated in Exodus, rather than asserting royal ownership of the funds.
The later comparison with Antiochus explicitly recalls the divine scourging that stopped Heliodorus's advance against the treasury.
The splendid rider with golden armour resembles the later horseman bearing golden armour who leads the defenders; the first manifestation attacks Heliodorus and the second aids Judas.
The two young men who scourge Heliodorus are explicitly described as the same figures when they return to explain his restored life and commission his testimony.
Heliodorus's fall and removal on a litter resemble Antiochus's later public humiliation and helpless transport on a litter; the men and injuries differ.
Heliodorus's helpless removal is the event later recalled when the narrator says he was scourged and thrown back from his rash advance.
Heliodorus's apparent loss of every hope of rescue is reversed by the messengers' declaration that the Lord has granted him life through Onias.
The request that Onias pray for Heliodorus's life resembles God's direction that Abraham pray so that the threatened Abimelech may live; the offences and intercessors differ.
Onias's sacrifice for Heliodorus's deliverance is answered by the explicit declaration that the Lord granted life because of Onias.
The returning young men are explicitly the same two splendid figures who had scourged Heliodorus, now announcing the reason for his recovery.
The command to proclaim God's majestic power is followed by Heliodorus's testimony to everyone about what he had witnessed.
Heliodorus's public witness carries out the heavenly figures' express command to proclaim God's power.
Heliodorus's warning that a hostile agent will be struck down at the temple resembles Darius's declaration that God will overthrow rulers who try to destroy His Jerusalem house.
The confession that God dwells in heaven yet protects this place resembles Solomon's repeated distinction between prayer toward the chosen house and God's hearing from His heavenly dwelling.
Simon's charge that Onias engineered Heliodorus's harm conflicts with the preceding account of Onias interceding for his life and the heavenly messengers crediting that intercession.
Onias's appeal to the king for the people's welfare continues his earlier concern to prevent the king from blaming the Jews for Heliodorus's injury.
Both narratives introduce the accession of Antiochus Epiphanes; 2 Maccabees connects it to Jason's displacement of Onias, while 1 Maccabees supplies the Seleucid year and royal ancestry.
Jason's promised payments for office are surpassed when Menelaus secures the priesthood by outbidding him, exposing the same financial mechanism in his displacement.
Both accounts connect royal permission for foreign customs with a gymnasium in Jerusalem; 2 Maccabees names Jason and states the proposed payment and civic registration.
Jason's royal authorization and turn toward Greek civic life correspond to the companion narrative's permission to follow foreign ordinances and abandonment of the covenant.
The description of Eupolemus son of John as envoy to Rome for friendship and alliance matches Judas's named Roman envoy in 1 Maccabees.
Both passages specifically describe the construction of a gymnasium in Jerusalem; the location beneath the citadel and the hat are details supplied here.
The narrator's condemnation of Jason's promotion of foreign ways corresponds to the companion account's judgment that the Hellenizing reform abandoned the holy covenant.

The warning that admired foreign rulers would become punishers anticipates Antiochus's assault on Jerusalem and plunder of the temple rather than treating the earlier cultural alliance as secure protection.
The warning that impiety against divine laws brings consequences is developed in the later explanation that the nation's disasters are divine discipline rather than abandonment.
Antiochus's splendid welcome in Jerusalem contrasts with his later violent seizure of the same city after he interprets the conflict as rebellion.
Menelaus's higher offer displaces Jason by the same purchase of royal approval through which Jason had obtained the priesthood.
The narrator's claim that Menelaus brings nothing worthy of the priesthood is exemplified when he guides Antiochus into the temple as a traitor to the laws and homeland.
Jason's loss of the priesthood explicitly reverses his fraudulent displacement of his brother Onias at the chapter's beginning.
Menelaus fails to make the payments by which he had outbid Jason and obtained the priesthood.
Lysimachus's appointment as Menelaus's deputy sets up his temple thefts, armed attack, and death beside the treasury under Menelaus's consent.
Menelaus's theft of sacred gold precedes his later role guiding Antiochus to remove the temple's vessels and royal gifts; the two episodes involve different seizures.

Andronicus draws Onias from safety with assurances and kills him, resembling Joab's drawing Abner aside for an apparently private conversation before killing him; the motives and asylum details differ.

The execution of Onias's deceitful murderer corresponds to the law requiring death for intentional killing and denying refuge to a deceitful murderer; Antiochus's procedure is not described as a formal application of that law.
Lysimachus's thefts with Menelaus's approval follow the explicit appointment of Lysimachus to act as deputy in the high priesthood.
Menelaus's promised payment to alter the king's judgment exemplifies the precise corruption of judgment prohibited by the law against bribes.
Ptolemy changes the king's mind after the promised payment, illustrating the law's warning that gifts corrupt just judgment.
The acquittal of Menelaus and execution of his accusers directly invert the law's prohibition on killing the innocent and justifying the ungodly for gifts.
The unjust execution of those defending the community and sacred vessels falls under the law's explicit prohibition on killing the innocent and righteous.
Menelaus's continued office through corrupt influence is later overturned when the king condemns him as the source of the evils and he dies in a manner interpreted as recompense for altar offences.
Both narratives describe Antiochus campaigning in Egypt; the present text explicitly calls this his second expedition, so the notices are not flattened into one dated campaign.
The visible supernatural horsemen resemble the horses and fiery chariot revealed around Elisha; the Jerusalem omen remains uncertain to its witnesses, unlike the explicit protection of Elisha.
Jason's attack on the city and Menelaus's flight follow the earlier account of Menelaus purchasing Jason's office and driving him away.
Jason's renewed flight into Ammonite territory expressly repeats the earlier destination after his displacement from the priesthood.
Jason's being hated as a deserter of the laws recalls the earlier account of his abolition of lawful customs and promotion of foreign practices.

Jason's hope of refuge among the Lacedaemonians on grounds of kinship corresponds to the Spartan letter's claim that Spartans and Jews are brothers descended from Abraham; it does not independently establish a personal family pedigree.
Both narratives place an armed advance against Jerusalem after Antiochus's Egyptian campaign; their dating and explanation of the trigger are retained separately.
The order for merciless killing supplies a detailed account alongside 1 Maccabees' report that Antiochus committed bloodshed after his intrusion into Jerusalem.
Both accounts describe Antiochus arrogantly entering the sanctuary; Menelaus's role as guide is supplied specifically by 2 Maccabees.
Both accounts explicitly describe the seizure of sacred vessels and precious objects from the Jerusalem temple.
The explanation that God briefly permits disaster because of the inhabitants' sins corresponds to the later statement that discipline does not mean God has abandoned His people.
The narrator expressly compares Antiochus's unopposed advance with Heliodorus's earlier divine scourging and helpless removal from the treasury.

The priority of God's choice of the nation recalls the law's account of Israel's election through divine love and faithfulness to the fathers; Deuteronomy does not itself make the comparison with the temple site.
The statement that the place later shared in the nation's renewed favour anticipates the recovery, cleansing, and renewed worship of the temple.
Both narratives describe Antiochus carrying away temple treasure and departing; the eighteen-hundred-talent total and return to Antioch are details of this account.
The king's fantasy of mastering land and sea is recalled when the later narrator describes the would-be commander of the waves reduced to helplessness on a litter.
Philip's appointment to afflict Jerusalem is exemplified by the report that concealed Sabbath observers were denounced to Philip and burned.
Menelaus's hostility toward fellow citizens continues when he joins the invading royal force and urges it on for his own restoration to office.

Both narratives describe a dispatched royal force devastating Jerusalem and taking women and children captive; the companion account calls its officer a chief tribute collector rather than naming Apollonius.
The officer's pretence of peaceful intent before a sudden assault matches the companion account's deceptive peaceful words; the Sabbath parade is additional detail here.
The armed rush against Jerusalem and killing of its inhabitants correspond to the sudden destructive attack after deceptive peaceful words in the companion account.
Judas's small band's retreat to mountain wilderness resembles the withdrawal of Mattathias's family and other refugees; the number and immediate leadership differ.
Both accounts describe royal enforcement of foreign customs designed to make the Jews abandon ancestral law.
The defilement and renaming of Jerusalem's temple correspond to the companion account's erection of the abomination upon the altar; the names Zeus and Gerizim appear only in this account.
The intrusion of forbidden practices into the sacred enclosure carries out the royal program of defiling the sanctuary and imposing pagan worship described in 1 Maccabees.
The altar's forbidden contents correspond to the companion decree requiring sacrifice of pigs and unclean animals.
Both accounts explicitly identify the profanation or obstruction of Sabbaths and ancestral festivals under the royal policy.
The enforced sacrificial participation belongs to the wider royal policy commanding sacrifice in the cities; the king's birthday and Dionysus procession are distinctive details here.
The decree to neighbouring Greek cities corresponds to the companion account's kingdom-wide royal instructions and local enforcement; Ptolemy's initiating role is specified here.
Both accounts expressly make death the sanction for refusal to adopt the king's prescribed customs.
Both accounts describe the execution of mothers who circumcised their children and infants hung from their bodies; 2 Maccabees specifies two women and their being thrown from the wall.

Both accounts describe hidden Sabbath observers killed while refusing self-defence; 2 Maccabees names Philip and burning, while 1 Maccabees gives the larger family company and a total of about a thousand.

The author's exhortation not to recoil from disasters but understand them as discipline resembles the wisdom instruction not to lose heart under the Lord's correction because He disciplines those He loves.
The interpretation of prompt punishment as kindness resembles Moses' description of the Lord chastening Israel as a father chastens a son, leading to obedience.
The contrast with nations whose punishment waits for sin's full measure recalls the explicit statement that the Amorites' sins were not yet filled up.
The assurance that disaster does not cancel God's mercy corresponds to the covenant promise not to reject or destroy His people even in their enemies' land.
The attempt to force Eleazar to eat pork directly conflicts with the law naming the pig unclean and forbidding its flesh.
Eleazar's deliberate choice of death rather than a defiled life exemplifies the companion account's description of those who died rather than eat unclean foods.
Eleazar's rejection of the forced food observes the explicit prohibition against eating pig flesh, even though the law itself does not narrate this martyrdom.
The proposal to substitute lawful meat while pretending compliance is rejected because Eleazar believes that visible pretence would mislead the young.
The offer of release from death resembles Hebrews' account of sufferers refusing release under torture; the comparison does not identify an unnamed person in Hebrews as Eleazar.
Eleazar's refusal to pretend addresses the precise proposal that he eat his own lawful meat while appearing to obey the king's sacrificial command.

Eleazar's concern that observers will be led astray by his apparent eating resembles Paul's warning that a person's visible eating can encourage another into wrongdoing; the legal and communal settings differ.

Eleazar distinguishes escape from human punishment from inescapable divine authority over life and death, resembling Jesus' distinction between killers of the body and the One with authority over body and soul.
Eleazar intends his death as a noble example for the young; the narrator closes by affirming that it became an example for the young and the wider nation.
The executioners' hostility explicitly reverses the goodwill of acquaintances who had offered a means of release from death.

relationship: Bodily suffering and fear of God
rationale: Eleazar accepts bodily pain because he fears God and speaks separately of his soul's gladness, corresponding to the distinction between bodily killers and God's greater authority.
The narrator's judgment that Eleazar left a noble example confirms Eleazar's expressly stated purpose before he went to the torture frame.
The pork forced upon the brothers is precisely the flesh the law declares unclean and forbids eating.
The brothers' readiness to die rather than violate ancestral law corresponds to the companion account's description of those who chose death rather than defilement by food.
The martyr's appeal to Moses' song and divine compassion for His servants corresponds to the song's declaration that the Lord will judge His people and be moved concerning His servants.
The promise of everlasting renewed life for those dying faithfully corresponds to Daniel's distinction between rising to everlasting life and rising to shame.

The brother's acceptance of death in hope of resurrection closely resembles the sufferers who refuse release under torture in hope of a better resurrection; no unnamed sufferer is individually identified.

The hope of receiving sacrificed bodily members again corresponds to Paul's account of the body raised from weakness and corruption; Paul develops the kind of resurrection body beyond this martyr's statement.

The distinction between resurrection to life for the faithful and its denial to the persecutor resembles Jesus' distinction between resurrection of life and resurrection of judgment, rather than denial that the wicked rise at all.
The martyr's denial that God has abandoned the people repeats the narrator's earlier explanation that discipline does not withdraw mercy or abandon Israel.
The threat that the king will experience divine torment anticipates the later account of his incurable pain and bodily decay; this target does not separately narrate punishment of his offspring.
The confession that suffering follows the people's sins adopts the narrator's preceding interpretation of disasters as discipline for impiety.
The warning that the persecutor will not escape punishment is followed by the narrator's explicit explanation that the king's bodily torment repays his torture of others.

The mother's hope while losing her sons can be compared with Hebrews' juxtaposition of women receiving their dead and tortured believers seeking a better resurrection; her sons are not restored during this scene.

relationship: Mystery of formation in the womb
rationale: The mother's inability to explain the formation and life of her children resembles the wisdom comparison between unknown formation in the womb and the mystery of God's works.
The mother's appeal to the Creator who formed humanity and can restore life recalls God's formation of the human being and gift of life in Genesis; resurrection is her further inference here.
The offer of wealth, royal friendship, and responsibility for abandoning ancestral ways closely resembles the offer of gifts and status as the king's Friends made to Mattathias and his sons.
The mother's agreement to persuade the boy leads to her urging him to accept death, reversing the king's intention that she persuade him to save his life by compliance.
The mother's appeal to God as maker of heaven and earth recalls Genesis' opening confession; her explicit statement about making them not from existing things goes beyond that verse's wording.
The mother's appeal to creation from what did not exist resembles Paul's joining of God's giving life to the dead with calling things that are not as though they are.
The mother urges acceptance of death in hope of receiving her children again, corresponding to the linked themes of restored children and refusal of release for a better resurrection in Hebrews.
The youngest brother's refusal of the king's ordinance in favour of Moses' law parallels Mattathias's refusal to obey royal words that require abandoning ancestral covenant and law.
The explicit choice of God's law over the king's ordinance resembles the apostles' statement that God must be obeyed rather than human authorities, in a different conflict.
The warning that the king cannot escape God's hands recalls the Mosaic song's declaration that no one can deliver from God's hands, already invoked earlier in the martyr scene.
The admission of suffering because of the people's own sins repeats the preceding explanation that their disasters correct impiety rather than signify abandonment.
The expectation that brief anger will end in reconciliation develops the narrator's assurance that divine discipline never removes mercy from God's own people.
The warning against the king's vain exaltation anticipates the later portrayal of his superhuman pretensions collapsed into helpless transport on a litter.
The warning of the all-seeing God's judgment anticipates the explicit statement that the all-seeing Lord strikes the king with an incurable plague.
The contrast between the brothers' everlasting life and the persecutor's punishment resembles Daniel's contrast between those raised to everlasting life and those raised to shame.

The request that trials make the king confess God's sole sovereignty is answered narratively by his recognition under divine scourging that a mortal must submit to God and not claim equality with Him.
The prayer that divine anger come to rest in the martyrs is followed by the narrator's declaration that the Lord's anger turned to mercy when Judas's resistance succeeded.
The king's increased cruelty belongs to the inflicted torments which the later narrator explicitly gives as the reason his own internal suffering is just recompense.
The youngest brother dies undefiled, exemplifying the companion account's description of those who chose death rather than defile themselves with food or profane the covenant.
The gathering of about six thousand develops the earlier account of Judas's withdrawal with only about nine companions into mountain wilderness.
Both accounts describe the resistance appealing to Heaven because the holy places are trampled and the people face destruction.
The appeal to blood crying to God recalls the description of Abel's blood crying from the ground after his murder.
The prayer's remembrance of innocent infants' destruction recalls the execution of circumcising mothers and their infants during the persecution.
The narrator's statement that anger turned to mercy follows the youngest martyr's prayer that the nation's deserved anger end with his and his brothers' suffering.
The raids, burning, and defeat of enemies resemble the companion summary of Judas pursuing lawless opponents and removing their presence from Judah's cities.
The spread of Judas's reputation corresponds to the companion account of terror among the nations and reports of his battles reaching the king; the use of night attacks is specified here.
Both accounts make reports of Judas's success the cause of stronger royal opposition; the present chain through Philip and Ptolemy differs from the companion account's emphasis on Antiochus.

Both accounts associate Ptolemy, Nicanor, and Gorgias with a force intended to destroy Judea; the command arrangement and figures differ, including twenty thousand here and forty thousand infantry in 1 Maccabees.
Nicanor's plan to finance the Roman tribute from Jewish captives is expressly recalled when he instead proclaims that the Jews have a divine Defender.
Both accounts describe merchants arriving to purchase Jewish captives in anticipation of victory; the fixed price and Nicanor's invitation are supplied here.
Both narratives describe Judas learning that the royal army is approaching to destroy the people before he prepares the resistance.

The departure of fearful men resembles Judas's earlier dismissal of the fearful according to the law, but this account characterizes their departure as distrust rather than repeating that legal procedure.
Both battle preparations include the remaining community's collective prayer for mercy and rescue; the sale of their remaining goods is specific to this account.
Both appeals for rescue expressly ask God to act because of the covenant with the fathers rather than confidence in the army's resources.
Judas's instruction not to fear a numerous attacking force follows the law's specific exhortation against fear before a larger enemy because God fights for Israel.
The exhortation to remember the sanctuary and the city's mistreatment corresponds to the companion call to fight for the people and holy places.
The contrast between enemies' military confidence and Israel's trust in God resembles the psalm's contrast between chariots and horses and reliance on the Lord's name.
Judas's confidence in God's power rather than weapons corresponds to his declaration in the companion account that battle strength comes from heaven rather than army size.
The recalled destruction of one hundred eighty-five thousand under Sennacherib is the event narrated when the Lord's angel strikes the Assyrian camp and the king departs.
The readiness to die for laws and homeland corresponds to the companion description of Judas's men fighting for their lives and customs; the four divisions are not specified there.
The reading of the sacred book before engagement resembles the companion preparation in which the book of the law is unrolled at the prebattle assembly.
Both narratives describe Judas defeating and pursuing the royal force, but the more-than-nine-thousand killed here differs from the companion account's approximately three thousand.

The victors' seizure of the buyers' money corresponds to the companion account's taking of abundant gold, silver, and wealth from the defeated camp; the companion passage does not specify each owner's trade.
The decision to stop pursuit before the Sabbath applies the command to sanctify the seventh day by ceasing ordinary work; the law does not narrate this campaign.
Both victory accounts move from taking spoils to blessing God and recognizing His mercy and deliverance; this account expressly connects the thanksgiving to Sabbath observance.
The victors' renewed appeal for full reconciliation continues the martyr's request that God quickly become merciful to the nation.
The equal shares for fighters and vulnerable noncombatants resemble David's rule of equal shares for fighters and those who remained with the equipment; the beneficiary groups differ.
The defeat of Timothy's forces belongs to the news about Timothy and Nicanor that subsequently reaches Antiochus at Ecbatana; the target does not separately name Bacchides.
The punishment of those who burned the sacred gateways recalls the companion account's inspection of the sanctuary with its gates burned down.
The narrator's mention of merchants brought to buy Jews recalls Nicanor's express invitation to the coastal cities and his proposed captive price.
Nicanor's solitary disguised retreat reverses his earlier advance with a large royal force and confident plans to sell the Jewish people.
The concluding account explicitly contrasts Nicanor's promised payment of Roman tribute from captives with his forced recognition of Israel's divine Defender.
